Anglo American has corrected the story the trade had settled on. Nobody has De Beers.

Duncan Wanblad, Anglo's chief executive, says the sale is in its final and hardest phase, that Anglo is not exclusive with any consortium, and that multiple bidders remain live. Completion is targeted for the second half of this year, with regulatory approval about a year after signature. That timetable runs well into 2027 before anyone new actually controls the company.

This desk carried the other version on July 26, under a headline saying Anglo had picked the group assembled by Gareth Penny. The clock was right. The pick was not, and we are saying so here rather than quietly. A named front-runner and a live auction produce very different prices for the same asset.

A listing is now formally excluded: Anglo does not believe the market can absorb a De Beers flotation. What replaces it is a private sale to a buyer under no duty to publish anything. A listed De Beers reports its rough index every quarter. A privately held one need not, and for sightholders funding rough through the winter that difference is not abstract.

The new tariff line does not run between two countries. It runs between two kinds of diamond.

Since July 24 the Section 301 schedule lets loose natural diamonds cut in the European Union enter the United States at 0%, exempted outright from the 10% to 12.5% duties applied to roughly sixty countries. Coloured stones and natural pearls from the bloc are exempt on the same terms. Lab-grown diamonds got no exemption from any country on the list.

The mechanism explains the shape of it. Section 301 protects a domestic industry, and the United States has neither a diamond mine of consequence nor a cutting trade to shelter, so a duty on polished naturals would tax American retailers to defend nothing. The same logic exempted raw gold, silver, platinum and palladium. It did not exempt lab-grown, which the United States does manufacture.

Belgium shipped $2.1 billion of polished to the US in 2024, and now ships it duty-free. A grower in Surat ships at 10%. The lab-grown trade spent three years arguing it should be judged as a diamond rather than by where it came from. The customs schedule has obliged, using the more expensive definition.

Gold demand was flat. The bill was the largest ever recorded. Both are true, and the gap between them is the whole story.

The World Gold Council counted 1,269 tonnes in the second quarter, unchanged on a year earlier, and 2,522 tonnes across the half, up 2%. Measured in money rather than metal, that same half-year was worth roughly $380 billion, a record. The tonnage moved two percentage points. The value moved to an all-time high.

Underneath is a straight substitution. Central banks took 289 tonnes, up 62%. Jewellery fabrication fell to 278 tonnes, the weakest quarter since the pandemic, with India down 15% by weight even as the value of Indian demand rose about 50%. Institutions bought weight. Consumers bought less weight and paid more for it, and the aggregate held flat only because the two cancelled almost exactly.

For anyone replacing sold stock that is not an abstraction: the same case, the same number of pieces, a substantially larger cheque. Report the tonnage to understand demand and the value to understand your own accounts, and never let the two be quoted in the same sentence without a note.
